description.en: The around the world superman hold combines a prone superman with arm sweeps. The arms sweep in a circular path from overhead, out wide, and back to the hips while the chest stays lifted.

en: Lie face down on the floor with legs straight and arms overhead.
Lift the chest, arms, and legs off the floor into a superman position.
Brace the core and squeeze the glutes to support the back.
Sweep the arms wide out to the sides at shoulder height.
Continue sweeping the arms back along the body to the hips.
Reverse the path back to the wide position.
Sweep the arms forward overhead to the start.
Maintain the lifted superman position throughout the full sweep.
Hammers the upper back through the full sweep.
Strengthens the rear deltoids and rhomboids.
Trains the spinal erectors with the superman hold.
Improves shoulder mobility through full range.
No equipment needed.
Excellent posture and back health drill.

description.en: The band lying hip external rotation is a clamshell variation that uses a resistance band looped around the knees. The mover rotates the top knee away while keeping the feet together. It is a strong glute medius and hip rotator builder.

en: Loop a resistance band around the knees.
Lie on one side with the knees bent at ninety degrees.
Stack the hips and shoulders.
Brace your core and keep the feet together.
Rotate the top knee away from the bottom knee.
Open the knees against the band tension.
Squeeze the glute hard at the top.
Lower with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Builds the glute medius
Trains the hip rotators
Strong hip stability move
Useful warm-up
Builds the glutes

description.en: The band lying straight leg raise adds resistance to the basic leg raise. The lifter lies on the back with a band looped around the feet and the other end anchored low. The lifter raises the straight legs against the band tension to load the hip flexors and abs.

en: Anchor a resistance band low to a sturdy point.
Loop the other end around both feet together.
Lie flat on the back with the legs extended and feet pointing toward the anchor.
Place the hands at the sides for support.
Brace your core hard.
Raise both legs straight up to vertical against the band tension.
Squeeze the abs hard at the top.
Lower the legs back down with control to the start.
Strong hip flexor builder
Adds resistance to leg raises
Builds the abs
Useful core builder
Strong band move
Builds the rectus abdominis

description.en: The band skull crusher is a lying tricep extension where you anchor a resistance band behind your head and extend at the elbows from a lying position. It mimics the barbell skull crusher with band tension, providing increasing resistance at lockout.

en: Anchor a resistance band at a low point behind your head.
Lie on your back. Grip both ends of the band overhead with palms facing forward.
Start with elbows bent, band behind your head (like the bottom of a skull crusher).
Extend your elbows to press the band straight up to lockout.
Squeeze your triceps at the top.
Slowly bend your elbows to lower the band back behind your head.
Keep your upper arms vertical throughout.
Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Mimics skull crushers at home
Increasing band tension at lockout
Builds tricep size and strength
Highly portable
Easy to scale
Joint-friendly

description.en: The barbell banded squat adds resistance bands attached to the floor or a rack to a standard back squat. The bands stretch as you stand, creating accommodating resistance that gets heavier toward the top of the lift. This forces explosive drive out of the hole and builds lockout strength.

en: Set up a barbell in a power rack with bands anchored to the floor or to the bottom of the rack.
Loop the bands over each end of the barbell.
Step under the bar and place it across your upper back, gripping it firmly.
Unrack the bar and step back into your squat stance.
Brace your core, sit back, and squat down to depth.
Drive up through your heels with explosive force, fighting against the band tension.
Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended.
The bands should reach maximum tension at the top of the lift.
Accommodating resistance gets harder as leverage improves
Builds explosive drive out of the bottom
Develops lockout strength
Trains acceleration through the entire range
Common method in conjugate-style powerlifting
Forces fast, intentional concentric drive

description.en: The barbell bench squat (similar to the box squat) is a back squat performed by squatting down to lightly touch a bench positioned behind you. The bench provides a consistent depth target and forces you to sit back into your hips, building posterior chain involvement.

en: Place a flat bench behind you in a power rack. Set the barbell on the rack.
Unrack the bar across your upper traps. Step back so the bench is just behind your heels.
Set feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out.
Sit your hips back and down. Squat down until your glutes lightly touch the bench.
Do NOT collapse onto the bench — just touch and stand.
Drive through your feet to stand back up.
Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Use moderate to heavy weight. Aim for 5 to 8 reps.
Consistent depth from bench reference
Forces sitting back into hips
Builds posterior chain involvement
Easier to learn proper depth
Useful powerlifting accessory
Builds glute drive out of the hole

description.en: The barbell pullover is a classic lat and chest exercise where you lie on a flat bench and arc a barbell from over your chest to behind your head. The lats and chest stretch deeply at the bottom and contract together as you pull the bar back over. It builds lat width and ribcage expansion.

en: Lie on a flat bench. Hold a barbell with a shoulder-width overhand grip above your chest, arms extended.
Keep a slight bend in your elbows throughout.
Slowly arc the bar behind your head and toward the floor.
Lower until you feel a deep stretch in your lats and chest.
Pull the bar back over to above your chest in a wide arc.
Squeeze your lats and chest at the top.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Old-school bodybuilding favorite for chest and back development.
Builds lat width and chest size simultaneously
Deep stretch through chest and lats
Old-school bodybuilding exercise
Develops shoulder flexibility
Builds the serratus anterior
Useful for chest and back development

description.en: The barbell squat with a 2 second hold is a pause squat variation where you hold the bottom position for a full two seconds before standing. The pause eliminates any rebound from the stretch reflex, building raw concentric strength out of the hole and reinforcing strict bottom-position bracing.

en: Set up under a barbell in a power rack with the bar across your upper back.
Step back and stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core and lift your chest.
Squat down by sitting back and bending the knees to depth.
Hold the bottom position for a full two seconds with tight bracing.
Maintain an upright torso and tight core throughout the pause.
Drive up explosively from the dead-stop bottom position.
Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended.
Builds positional strength at the bottom
Eliminates the stretch reflex
Develops time under tension at the hardest position
Forces strict bracing and form
Strong carryover to competition squat
Useful for breaking through squat sticking points

description.en: The bench reverse crunch circle is a reverse crunch variation with a leg circle. The lifter lies on a flat bench and circles the legs in big circles while reverse crunching the hips up. The circle adds dynamic oblique work to the reverse crunch.

en: Lie on your back on a flat bench.
Grip the bench overhead behind your head with both hands.
Lift the legs straight up toward the ceiling.
Brace your core hard.
Begin circling the legs in big circles in the air.
At the top of each circle reverse crunch the hips up off the bench.
Lower the hips back down as the legs continue the circle.
Continue circles in one direction. Reverse and repeat.
Strong abs builder
Adds dynamic oblique work
Trains the hip flexors
Builds full core strength
Useful core finisher
Strong reverse crunch variation

description.en: The bent-knee side plank holds a side plank with knees bent on the floor rather than on the feet. The shortened lever makes it significantly easier — a regression for those who cannot hold a full side plank.

en: Lie on your right side. Bend both knees at 90 degrees.
Place your right forearm on the floor, elbow under shoulder.
Lift your hips off the floor. Support yourself on your forearm and knees.
Body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Hold for 15 to 30 seconds.
Switch sides.
The bent knees shorten the lever — much easier than full side plank.
Progress to full side plank on feet when ready.
Beginner regression for side planks
Shortened lever reduces difficulty
Builds oblique endurance for beginners
No equipment needed
Progressive toward full side plank
Safe and accessible

description.en: The bodyweight bent over rear delt fly is a no equipment activation drill. From a bent over stance, you sweep the arms out to the sides like a fly to fire the rear delts and upper back.

en: Stand with the feet shoulder width apart.
Hinge at the hips until the torso is roughly parallel to the floor.
Allow the arms to hang straight down with palms facing each other.
Brace the core and keep the back flat.
Sweep the arms out to the sides by squeezing the shoulder blades.
Stop at shoulder height with thumbs pointing up.
Squeeze the rear delts and traps at the top.
Lower the arms back down with control and repeat.
Activates the rear delts and upper back.
No equipment needed.
Excellent warm up before pressing or pulling.
Builds upper back posture.
Carryover to face pulls and reverse flys.
Reduces upper back stiffness.

description.en: The bodyweight frog hip thrust is a hip thrust style move where the soles of the feet are pressed together with the knees out wide. The frog position shifts emphasis to the outer glutes and adductors. It is a strong bodyweight glute builder.

en: Sit on the floor with the soles of your feet pressed together.
Let your knees fall out wide.
Place your upper back against a sturdy bench.
Brace your core and keep your chin tucked.
Drive through the outer edges of your feet to lift your hips up.
Reach a flat hip position with the body in a tabletop.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top.
Lower the hips back down with control.
Builds outer glutes
Trains adductor strength
No equipment required
Strong bodyweight glute move
Hits glute medius
Useful at-home option

description.en: The bodyweight incline side plank is a regression of the side plank for trainees who cannot hold a full side plank. The lifter places the bottom hand on a bench with feet on the floor in a side plank position. The incline reduces the load and is a strong oblique builder.

en: Set up a sturdy bench or low surface.
Place one hand on the edge of the bench.
Walk the feet out to the side until the body is in a straight line.
Stack the feet or place the top foot in front for stability.
Brace your core and squeeze the bottom obliques.
Hold the body in a straight diagonal line.
Reach the top arm up to the ceiling for full effect.
Hold the position for time. Switch sides and repeat.
Beginner friendly oblique move
Builds shoulder stability
No equipment beyond a bench
Strong core builder
Useful side plank progression
Easy to scale by incline

description.en: The cable lying upright row is performed lying on your back on the floor with cables attached to a low pulley below your feet. Pulling the handle up from your hips toward your chin trains the shoulders and traps. The lying position changes the angle of pull and reduces the shoulder strain associated with standing upright rows.

en: Set a cable to the lowest pulley with a single bar or rope attachment.
Lie on your back on the floor with feet toward the cable.
Grip the bar with both hands at thigh level with arms extended.
Brace your core and press your back to the floor.
Pull the bar up toward your chin by leading with the elbows.
Lift your elbows out to the sides as the bar travels up.
Continue until the bar reaches chest level.
Slowly lower the bar back down with control.
Shoulder-friendlier than standing upright rows
Constant cable tension through the range
Lying position eliminates body english
Builds shoulder and trap strength
Different angle than standing variations
Useful for breaking through shoulder plateaus

description.en: The cable one arm wrist curl is performed kneeling at a low cable station with a single handle. With the forearm braced on a bench and the cable handle in hand, you curl by flexing only the wrist. The cable tension and bench support combine for strict single-arm forearm flexor work.

en: Set a cable to the lowest pulley with a single handle.
Kneel beside a flat bench with the cable in front of you.
Drape your right forearm over the bench top with palm facing up.
Grip the cable handle with your right hand and let your wrist hang off the bench.
Brace your core.
Lower your wrist by extending it down toward the floor.
Curl the cable up by flexing your wrist.
Squeeze your forearm at the top, then lower with control. Switch arms.
Single-arm forearm isolation
Constant cable tension through the range
Bench support eliminates body english
Builds grip strength
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strict isolation

description.en: The cable triceps pushdown on floor is a kneeling pushdown variation. The lifter kneels under a high cable and pushes the attachment all the way down to the floor in front. The kneeling angle and floor finish position add a strong squeeze at lockout.

en: Set a cable to a high position with a straight or rope attachment.
Kneel directly under the cable on both knees.
Grip the attachment with both hands.
Set the elbows tight against the sides.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Push the attachment straight down to the floor.
Squeeze the triceps hard at full lockout.
Allow the elbows to bend back to the start with control.
Strong tricep builder
Unique kneeling angle
Strong lockout squeeze
Constant cable tension
Useful arm builder
Strong cable move

description.en: The cable upright row is a vertical pulling exercise performed at a low cable pulley. You pull the cable attachment up the front of your body by driving your elbows up and out. The constant cable tension provides a smooth stimulus throughout the range, and the cable allows a more natural pull path than a barbell.

en: Attach a straight bar or EZ bar to a low cable pulley.
Stand facing the cable with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar shoulder-width or slightly wider.
Stand tall with the bar at arm’s length in front of your thighs. Brace your core.
Pull the bar up the front of your body by driving your elbows up and out.
Continue pulling until the bar reaches roughly chest height. Your elbows should be at or slightly above shoulder height.
Do not pull higher than chest level to protect the shoulders.
Pause briefly, then lower under control. Maintain cable tension throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Constant cable tension throughout the range of motion
Smoother pull path than barbell upright rows
Builds the upper traps and lateral delts together
Easy to load progressively in small increments
Multiple attachment options for different stimuli
Excellent for high-rep shoulder volume

description.en: The double kneeling shin stretch is a seated stretch where you kneel with both feet pointed back (tops of feet on the floor) and sit back onto your heels. It deeply stretches the tibialis anterior (front of shin), tops of the feet, and ankles. It is one of the few effective stretches for the front of the shin.

en: Kneel on the floor with knees together. Point your feet straight back, with the tops of your feet pressing into the floor.
Sit back onto your heels. Your hips should rest on top of your heels.
Place your hands on your thighs or at your sides for support.
Sit up tall.
Feel the stretch through the front of your shins, tops of your feet, and ankles.
To deepen, lean back slightly while supporting your weight on your hands behind you.
Hold for 20 to 45 seconds. Breathe deeply.
To exit, lean forward and lift your hips off your heels carefully.
Stretches the often-neglected tibialis anterior
Opens the tops of the feet and ankles
Useful for runners with shin tightness
Helps with shin splint prevention
No equipment needed
Easy to integrate into mobility routines

description.en: The dumbbell 4 ways lateral raise combines four directional raises into one complex set: front raise, lateral raise, bent over rear delt raise, and Y raise. The combination hits all three deltoid heads with multiple angles in a single sequence, building total shoulder development with strong time under tension.

en: Stand with a light dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing your body.
Begin with a front raise: lift the dumbbells forward to shoulder height, then lower.
Continue with a lateral raise: lift the dumbbells out to the sides to shoulder height, then lower.
Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back.
Perform a bent over rear delt raise: lift the dumbbells out to the sides while bent over.
Stand back up and finish with a Y raise: lift the dumbbells up and forward at a 45-degree angle.
That sequence is one rep of the four-way raise.
Continue cycling through the four directions for the full set.
Hits all three deltoid heads in one set
Strong time under tension
Builds total shoulder development
Time-efficient compound shoulder movement
Useful for hypertrophy training
Strong shoulder pre-fatigue

description.en: The dumbbell lying on floor chest press (DB floor press) is a pressing variation performed lying flat on the floor. The floor limits the range at the bottom, stopping the elbows at ground level. This eliminates bottom-range shoulder stress and builds tricep lockout strength.

en: Lie on the floor with dumbbells in each hand at your shoulders.
Bend your knees with feet flat, or extend legs straight.
Press both dumbbells up to lockout above your chest.
Lower under control until your elbows touch the floor. Pause briefly.
Press back up to lockout.
The floor stops your elbows — eliminating the bottom stretch.
Builds tricep and lockout strength.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Floor limits range for shoulder safety
Builds tricep and lockout strength
No bench needed
Dead-stop at bottom removes stretch reflex
Useful at-home chest exercise
Easy setup

description.en: The dumbbell single stiff-leg deadlift performs a single-leg Romanian deadlift with minimal knee bend, maximizing hamstring involvement. You balance on one leg while hinging at the hips and lowering a dumbbell toward the floor. It builds unilateral hamstring strength and balance.

en: Stand holding a dumbbell in your right hand.
Shift your weight to your left leg. Keep a very slight bend in your left knee.
Hinge at the hips. Extend your right leg straight back as your torso lowers forward.
Lower the dumbbell toward the floor. Keep your back flat.
Continue until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor.
Drive your left hip forward to return to standing.
Squeeze your left glute at the top.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Builds unilateral hamstring and glute strength
Minimal knee bend maximizes hamstring involvement
Develops balance and proprioception
Exposes left-right imbalances
Simple setup
Builds hip hinge pattern on one leg

description.en: The elbow push-up is a unique pressing exercise where you start in a forearm plank position and press up to a high plank by extending at the elbows. The short range of motion heavily targets the triceps and forces tremendous core engagement to maintain the body line throughout the transition.

en: Start in a forearm plank position — elbows under shoulders, body in a straight line from heels to head.
Brace your core hard. Squeeze your glutes.
Press your right palm into the floor and extend your right arm to high plank.
Press your left palm into the floor and extend your left arm. You are now in a full high plank.
Lower back down by bringing your right elbow to the floor, then your left elbow.
You return to the forearm plank position.
Repeat. Alternate which arm leads each rep for balanced loading.
Maintain a perfectly straight body line throughout — no hip rocking or sagging.
Heavy tricep engagement through partial range
Tremendous anti-rotation core demand
Trains the transition between forearm and high plank
No equipment needed
Builds core strength and stability
Excellent finisher for upper body or core workouts

description.en: The exercise ball back extension with knees off ground is an advanced back extension done with the legs straight and only the toes contacting the floor. The lifted knee position increases the load on the glutes and hamstrings.

en: Lie face down with the hips supported on a stability ball.
Walk the feet back so the legs are straight.
Set the toes wide on the floor with the knees off the ground.
Place the hands by the ears or crossed on the chest.
Brace the core and keep the body relaxed at the start.
Lift the chest off the ball by extending the back.
Squeeze the glutes and hamstrings hard at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Builds the lower back.
Hammers the glutes and hamstrings.
Knees off floor adds load.
Joint friendly back work.
Useful for posterior chain.

description.en: The hanging leg hip raise is an advanced core exercise where you hang from a pull-up bar and lift your legs while curling your hips up toward your chest. The hip curl at the top differentiates it from a standard hanging leg raise — it forces the lower abs to do real work rather than letting the hip flexors take over. It is one of the most effective lower-ab builders.

en: Hang from a sturdy pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Pull your shoulders down and back to engage your lats. Brace your core.
Keep your legs straight (or slightly bent if you cannot do it with straight legs).
Lift your legs up toward your chest by contracting your hip flexors and abs.
As your thighs approach parallel to the floor, continue the movement by curling your hips up and back. Your tailbone should rotate up toward your chest.
At the peak, your hips should be flexed and your lower back rounded. Squeeze your lower abs hard.
Lower your legs slowly under control over two to three seconds back to the hanging start position.
Avoid swinging. If you cannot do strict reps, regress to bent-knee versions or hanging knee raises until you build the strength.
Builds the lower abs more effectively than floor-based exercises
The hip curl forces real ab work, not just hip flexor work
Trains grip and shoulder stability through the hang
Excellent advanced core exercise
Improves overall body control and coordination
Strong predictor of relative core strength

description.en: The high knee lunge on Bosu ball is a single leg balance and strength move with the back foot on a Bosu ball. The unstable back foot challenges balance while the high knee adds dynamic loading.

en: Place a Bosu ball about a stride length behind you.
Step the back foot onto the dome of the Bosu.
Lower into a deep lunge with the front shin vertical.
Brace the core and keep the chest tall.
Drive through the front foot to stand up tall.
Lift the back leg through into a high knee.
Pause briefly with the knee high and the body upright.
Lower the back leg back onto the Bosu and repeat then switch sides.
Builds single leg strength on an unstable surface.
Trains balance and proprioception.
Hammers the glutes and quads.
Improves athletic stability.
Develops core control.
Adds variety to standard lunges.

description.en: The kettlebell dead bug adds external load to the standard dead bug by holding a kettlebell locked out overhead. The weight pulls your arms toward the floor, creating a much greater anti-extension demand on the core. It is an advanced progression of the bodyweight dead bug.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees, feet off the floor.
Hold a light kettlebell with both hands, arms extended straight above your chest.
Press your lower back firmly into the floor. Brace your core.
Slowly extend your right leg straight forward, lowering it toward the floor. Keep your left knee at 90.
Simultaneously, keep the kettlebell locked out overhead — resist the pull.
Return your right leg to the starting position. Repeat with the left leg.
Alternate legs for the desired reps. Maintain lower back contact with the floor.
If your lower back arches off the floor, the weight is too heavy.
Greater anti-extension demand than bodyweight dead bug
Builds deep core stability
Excellent rehabilitation and strength exercise
Teaches bracing under load
Easy to scale by kettlebell weight
Improves lower-back health

description.en: The kettlebell goblet squat jump combines a goblet squat with an explosive jump out of the bottom. Holding a kettlebell at the chest adds load to the squat and the jump, training lower body power under resistance. The combo builds explosive strength and conditioning together.

en: Hold a kettlebell at your chest by the horns with both hands.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core and pull your elbows down to keep the kettlebell tight.
Squat down by bending your knees and pushing your hips back.
Continue down until your thighs are parallel to the floor.
Drive up explosively, jumping off the floor with the kettlebell still at your chest.
Land softly on the balls of your feet with knees slightly bent.
Immediately lower into the next squat. Continue for the duration of the set.
Trains loaded plyometric power
Builds explosive lower body strength
Strong cardiovascular component
Develops landing mechanics under load
Time-efficient power and conditioning combo
Functional carryover to athletic jumping

description.en: The kettlebell Sots press is an advanced mobility exercise where you sit at the bottom of a full squat and press a kettlebell overhead from that position. It demands extreme shoulder, thoracic, ankle, and hip mobility simultaneously. It is named after Soviet weightlifter Viktor Sots.

en: Clean a light kettlebell to the front rack position.
Squat down to full depth — as deep as you can go. Stay at the bottom.
From the bottom of the squat, press the kettlebell overhead to lockout.
Keep your torso as upright as possible. Core braced hard.
Lock out overhead with bicep near your ear.
Lower the kettlebell back to the front rack while remaining at the bottom of the squat.
Complete reps from the squat position, then stand up.
Use very light weight. This is a mobility exercise first, a strength exercise second.
Tests and builds extreme shoulder mobility
Demands thoracic, hip, and ankle flexibility
Improves overhead pressing position
Builds core stability under mobility demand
Named after Soviet weightlifter Viktor Sots
Excellent mobility assessment

description.en: The kettlebell Turkish get up to hand is a partial Turkish get up that stops at the elbow to hand transition. The move builds shoulder stability, hip mobility, and full body coordination.

en: Lie on your back with a kettlebell pressed up over the chest with one arm.
Bend the same side knee and plant the foot flat on the floor.
Extend the opposite arm and leg out at about 45 degrees.
Brace the core and keep the kettlebell pressed straight up.
Roll up onto the off side elbow while keeping the bell vertical.
Press up further onto the off side hand with the arm extended.
Pause briefly in the up to hand position with the kettlebell overhead.
Reverse the motion to lower back to the floor and complete all reps then switch.
Builds shoulder stability through the overhead carry.
Improves total body coordination.
Strengthens the core and obliques through the rolling motion.
Trains hip mobility through the leg drive.
Develops the deep stabilizers around the shoulder.
Excellent warm up or shoulder health drill.

description.en: The kneeling assisted sliding chin up is a regression of the strict chin up using the knees on the floor for assistance. The lifter grips a low bar with an underhand grip and pulls up while the knees slide along the floor. It is a useful chin up progression.

en: Set a sturdy bar at chest height.
Kneel on the floor under the bar.
Reach up and grip the bar with an underhand chin up grip.
Set the body in a straight line from knees to head.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades.
Pull the chest up toward the bar using the legs to assist.
Slide the knees along the floor as you pull up.
Lower back down with control to the start.
Beginner friendly chin up
Builds the lats
Trains the biceps
Useful chin up progression
No high bar needed
Builds back size

description.en: The L-sit on floor is an isometric core exercise where you sit on the floor, press down with your hands on either side of your hips, and lift your entire body off the floor with legs extended straight in front of you. It demands exceptional core, hip-flexor, and tricep strength. It is a foundational gymnastics hold and an advanced bodyweight exercise.

en: Sit on the floor with legs extended straight in front of you. Place your hands flat on the floor directly beside your hips, fingers pointing forward.
Press down through your palms and straighten your arms to lift your body off the floor. Your butt and legs should both clear the floor.
Keep your legs extended straight in front of you, parallel to the floor, forming an “L” shape with your torso.
Brace your core hard. Squeeze your quads to keep your legs straight. Point your toes forward.
Pull your shoulders down and back. Avoid shrugging.
Hold for the desired duration — even a few seconds is an accomplishment. Build up to 15 to 30 seconds.
If the full version is too difficult, start with tucked knees (tuck L-sit) or lift one leg at a time.
Using parallettes or raised surfaces makes this easier by giving more hand clearance.
Builds elite core, hip-flexor, and tricep strength
Foundational gymnastics skill
Trains the abs isometrically through a long lever arm
Develops shoulder depression and scapular control
No equipment needed (or use parallettes for easier version)
Excellent test of relative strength

description.en: The lean planche is a calisthenics progression toward the full planche. From a push-up position, you lean your body forward so your shoulders travel past your hands, shifting your center of gravity onto your palms. The more you lean, the closer the position approaches a planche. It builds shoulder, core, and wrist strength.

en: Start in a high plank position with hands shoulder-width apart on the floor.
Turn your hands outward slightly (fingers pointing to the sides) to protect your wrists.
Brace your core hard. Squeeze your glutes. Protract your shoulders (push the floor away).
Lean your body forward by shifting weight onto your hands — your shoulders should pass over or beyond your wrists.
Maintain straight arms and a straight body line.
Hold the forward-leaned position for 10 to 30 seconds.
Increase the forward lean gradually over weeks.
Your feet will become lighter. Eventually, they begin to lift as you approach planche balance.
Foundational planche progression
Builds extreme anterior deltoid strength
Develops wrist and forearm conditioning
Builds core bracing under forward lean
No equipment needed
Essential stepping stone to full planche

description.en: The lying double legs biceps curl with towel is a creative no equipment biceps move. Lying down and curling a towel against the resistance of both legs creates a self loaded biceps training stimulus.

en: Lie flat on your back on the floor with knees bent.
Loop a towel under both feet with each end held in your hands.
Set the elbows close to the body with palms facing up.
Press both legs gently against the towel to create tension.
Curl your hands up toward the shoulders by bending the elbows.
Increase or decrease leg pressure to control the load.
Squeeze the biceps at the top.
Lower the towel slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Trains the biceps with no weights needed.
Self regulating resistance from your own legs.
Joint friendly with smooth manual tension.
Excellent travel friendly biceps option.
Engages forearms through the towel grip.
Builds biceps endurance with high rep work.

description.en: The lying flat hip raise is a reverse crunch variation with the legs straight up. The lifter lies on the back with the legs vertical and lifts the hips off the floor by pressing the feet up. The vertical leg position isolates the lower abs.

en: Lie on your back on the floor.
Lift the legs straight up to vertical with feet pointing at the ceiling.
Place the hands at the sides for support.
Brace your core hard.
Press the feet up toward the ceiling lifting the hips off the floor.
Continue lifting until the hips are clear of the floor.
Squeeze the lower abs hard at the top.
Lower the hips back down with control.
Strong lower abs builder
No equipment needed
Trains the glutes
Builds the rectus abdominis
Useful core builder
Easy to do anywhere

description.en: The lying floor row with bent knee is a creative bodyweight back exercise. Hooking the hands under a sturdy fixed object and rowing the chest up off the floor with knees bent works the back without weights.

en: Find a sturdy fixed object low to the ground like a heavy bed or couch base.
Lie face up on the floor with the head and shoulders just past the object.
Reach back and grip the underside or edge with both hands.
Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor.
Brace the core and keep the body relatively straight.
Pull the chest up by driving the elbows back along the sides.
Squeeze the upper back at the top of the pull.
Lower yourself slowly back to the floor and repeat.
Trains horizontal pulling with no equipment.
Bent knees keep it accessible for beginners.
Strengthens the lats and mid back.
Builds biceps and grip strength.
Travel friendly with creative use of furniture.
No spinal compression like with bent over rows.

description.en: The lying leg hip raise on floor is a bodyweight ab move done lying flat. Lifting the legs and hips together off the floor in a reverse crunch motion shortens the abs hard and loads the lower portion of the rectus abdominis.

en: Lie on the back with the legs extended.
Place the arms at the sides palms down.
Brace the core and press the lower back into the floor.
Lift the legs straight up to vertical.
Continue lifting by curling the hips off the floor.
Drive the toes toward the ceiling at the top.
Squeeze the abs hard at the peak.
Lower with control to the start.
Loads the lower abs hard.
Trains the hip flexors.
Bodyweight move requires no equipment.
Builds the rectus abdominis.
Useful core finisher.

description.en: The lying scissors cross is a core exercise performed lying on the back with the legs lifted off the floor. The lifter crosses the straight legs over each other in a scissor pattern. The continuous crossing loads the lower abs and hip flexors.

en: Lie flat on your back on the floor.
Place your hands at your sides or under your hips.
Lift both legs off the floor a few inches.
Keep the legs straight and brace your core hard.
Cross one leg over the other in a scissor motion.
Uncross and cross the other leg over.
Continue alternating crosses with control.
Keep the lower back pressed into the floor.
Loads the lower abs
Builds hip flexor strength
No equipment needed
Easy to scale
Useful ab finisher
Strong basic ab move

description.en: The lying single leg circle is a Pilates mat exercise where you lie on your back and trace circles in the air with one extended leg while keeping the rest of your body completely still. It improves hip mobility, builds core stability, and trains the core to resist movement initiated from the limbs.

en: Lie flat on your back. Extend both legs straight along the floor.
Lift your right leg straight up toward the ceiling. Point your toes.
Press your lower back into the floor. Brace your core hard.
Trace small, controlled circles in the air with your right leg. Keep the rest of your body still.
Perform 5 to 8 circles in one direction, then reverse for 5 to 8 circles.
The non-working leg stays pressed flat on the floor throughout.
Switch to the left leg and repeat.
Start with small circles. Increase the size only if you can keep your hips and lower back stable.
Improves hip mobility through full circular range
Builds core stability against limb movement
Foundational Pilates mat exercise
Trains hip dissociation from the lower back
No equipment needed
Excellent rehabilitation exercise

description.en: The lever lying t bar row is a chest-supported version of the T-bar row performed face down on a machine pad. The chest support eliminates lower back loading and forces the upper back to do all the work. It is a top choice for back hypertrophy.

en: Lie face down on the lever T-bar row machine with chest on the pad.
Plant your feet on the foot platform and pin your hips down.
Grip the handles with palms facing each other.
Brace your core and let your arms hang down fully.
Row the handles toward your ribs by driving the elbows back.
Squeeze the upper back hard at the top of the row.
Lower with control until arms are straight again.
Keep your chest pinned to the pad throughout.
Removes lower back stress
Builds upper back size
Strict chest-supported form
Excellent back hypertrophy move
Easy to load heavy
Strong back day staple

description.en: The lever one arm lateral high row is a unilateral high row on a lever pulldown style machine. The lifter sits and grips a single handle, then pulls it down and back with one arm. The single arm work isolates one lat at a time and builds back size symmetrically.

en: Sit on a lever high row machine with the chest pad against the body.
Grip a single handle with one hand.
Set the arm extended up and out at the start.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blade.
Pull the handle down and back driving the elbow past the body.
Squeeze the lat hard at the bottom.
Return with control to the start.
Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong unilateral lat builder
Builds back symmetry
Trains the rhomboids
Builds back size
Useful back move
Strong machine move

description.en: The old school reverse extensions is a classic posterior chain builder using just a bench. The lifter lies face down on the bench with the hips at the edge and the legs hanging off. The lifter then lifts the straight legs up behind the body to load the glutes and lower back.

en: Lie face down on a flat bench with the hips at the edge.
Hold the bench with both hands for stability.
Let the legs hang straight down off the end of the bench.
Brace your core and squeeze the glutes.
Lift the straight legs up behind the body.
Continue lifting until the legs are parallel to the floor or higher.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top.
Lower the legs back down with control.
Strong posterior chain builder
No machine needed
Builds the glutes
Trains the lower back
Useful old school move
Builds the hamstrings

description.en: The rear deltoid stretch (also known as the cross-body shoulder stretch) is a classic upper-body stretch where you bring one arm across your body at chest height and use the opposite arm to gently pull it closer. It targets the rear deltoid, mid-traps, and rhomboids — all important muscles for shoulder health.

en: Stand or sit tall. Bring your right arm straight across your body at chest height, palm facing down.
Use your left arm to gently hook under your right arm at the elbow.
Pull your right arm closer to your chest with your left hand.
Feel the stretch through the back of your right shoulder.
Keep your right shoulder pulled down — do not let it shrug up toward your ear.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Switch sides and repeat.
Apply gentle pressure — never force the stretch.
Stretches the rear deltoid effectively
Opens the upper back and rhomboids
Quick and accessible
No equipment needed
Useful between sets or anytime during the day
Improves shoulder flexibility for overhead work

description.en: The ring rollout is an advanced core exercise where you grip gymnastic rings and extend your arms forward while maintaining a plank-like position, then pull back. The unstable rings add significantly more demand than an ab wheel, building elite anti-extension core strength and shoulder stability.

en: Set gymnastic rings at a low height (about knee level). Grip both rings.
Position yourself in a kneeling or standing plank with arms extended, gripping the rings.
Brace your core extremely hard. Tuck your pelvis.
Slowly extend the rings forward by pushing your arms forward and away from your body.
Continue extending until your body is nearly horizontal (or as far as your core can hold).
Do NOT let your lower back arch.
Pull yourself back to the starting position using your core and lats.
Master kneeling ring rollouts before attempting standing. Aim for 5 to 10 reps.
Elite anti-extension core builder
Rings add instability beyond ab wheel
Develops shoulder stability under extension
Builds lat and tricep strength
Advanced core progression
Carries over to all heavy lifting via core stability

description.en: The roll ball piriformis is a self myofascial release drill for the deep glute. Sitting on a small ball placed under the piriformis releases tightness from sitting and heavy lower body work.

en: Sit on the floor with a massage ball under one glute.
Stagger the legs with the working side leg crossed over.
Lean back onto the hands for support.
Brace the core and shift the weight onto the ball.
Roll the glute slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Stay deep in the glute near the hip joint.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the piriformis.
Improves hip rotation.
Reduces glute tightness.
Useful for desk workers.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The seated flutter kick holds a V-sit position (leaning back with legs elevated) and performs flutter kicks. The seated-back position adds upper ab demand from holding the torso while the flutter kicks target the lower abs and hip flexors.

en: Sit on the floor. Lean back to about 45 degrees. Support yourself with hands behind you or keep them at your sides.
Raise both legs 6 to 12 inches off the floor.
Alternately kick your legs up and down in a flutter pattern.
Keep kicks small and controlled — about 12 inches of travel.
Maintain the lean-back torso position throughout.
Breathe steadily.
Continue for 20 to 30 seconds or 15 to 25 kicks per leg.
Keep core braced throughout.
Sustained upper and lower ab tension
Combines V-sit hold with flutter kicks
No equipment needed
Builds core endurance
Targets abs from both upper and lower angles
Engaging variation

description.en: Shoulder Stand (Sarvangasana, "the queen of yoga poses") is a foundational inverted yoga pose where you balance on your shoulders with your legs extended straight up toward the ceiling. It is calming and restorative, improves circulation, and stimulates the thyroid. It demands neck health — modify or skip if you have neck issues.

en: Lie flat on your back with arms at your sides, palms down.
Bend your knees and bring them toward your chest. Press your hands into the floor.
Use a controlled rocking motion to lift your hips and lower back off the floor, swinging your knees overhead.
Bend your elbows and place your hands on your lower back to support your torso.
Slowly extend your legs straight up toward the ceiling. Body should be in a straight line from shoulders to toes.
Press your shoulders into the floor. Do not turn your head while in the pose.
Hold for 30 seconds to 2 minutes. Breathe deeply.
To exit, bend your knees and slowly roll down vertebra by vertebra.
Improves circulation through inversion
Calming and restorative
Stimulates the thyroid gland
Strengthens the shoulders, core, and upper back
Foundational inverted yoga pose
Reduces fatigue when held for moderate duration

description.en: The standing archer is a dynamic warm-up drill where you stand with feet wide and mimic the motion of drawing a bow — extending one arm forward while pulling the other back, rotating through the torso. It mobilizes the thoracic spine, warms up the shoulders, and builds rotational coordination.

en: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, in an athletic stance.
Extend your right arm straight forward at shoulder height, palm facing inward (like aiming a bow).
Bring your left hand up to your right shoulder and “draw the bow” — pull your left elbow back and across your body.
Rotate your torso to the left as you draw. Look forward over your right hand.
Hold for 1 to 2 seconds, then “release” by extending your left arm forward and switching the motion.
Repeat on the other side — left arm extends forward, right hand draws back.
Continue alternating in a rhythmic flow.
Perform for 30 to 60 seconds.
Mobilizes the thoracic spine through rotation
Warms up the shoulders
Builds rotational coordination
Excellent dynamic warm-up
No equipment needed
Engaging mobility drill

description.en: The standing hamstring stretch is a simple forward fold performed standing with both feet together or hip-width apart. You hinge at the hips and reach toward your toes, stretching the hamstrings, calves, and lower back. It is one of the most accessible flexibility exercises.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart or together.
Hinge forward at the hips, keeping a slight bend in your knees.
Reach toward your toes, shins, or the floor — wherever your flexibility allows.
Let your head hang heavy. Relax your neck.
Feel the stretch through your hamstrings and lower back.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
To deepen, gradually straighten the knees while keeping the back from rounding excessively.
Return to standing on an inhale with a flat back.
Stretches the hamstrings, calves, and lower back
Quick and accessible — works anywhere
Improves hip-hinge flexibility for deadlifts
Calming and restorative
No equipment needed
Easy to integrate into any cool-down

description.en: The standing hip abduction is a hip-isolation exercise where you lift one leg out to the side away from your body. The movement targets the gluteus medius and minimus — the muscles responsible for hip stability and the rounded outer shape of the glutes. It is a useful warm-up exercise and a building block for hip strength.

en: Stand tall with feet together, holding onto a wall, chair, or pole for balance.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Keep your supporting leg slightly soft (not locked).
Slowly lift your right leg out to the side by abducting at the hip. Keep your knee straight and your toes pointing forward.
Lift your leg to roughly 30 to 45 degrees from your body. Stop when you feel the contraction in your upper outer glute.
Avoid leaning your torso to the opposite side — keep your body upright. The work should come from the hip, not from leaning.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower the leg under control back to the start position.
Complete all reps on the right side, then switch to the left.
Add load by attaching ankle weights or a resistance band around the ankles for more challenge.
Direct gluteus medius and minimus activation
Improves hip stability and balance
Helps prevent knee and lower-back issues
No equipment needed — works anywhere
Excellent warm-up exercise
Builds the upper outer glute

description.en: The stick lat stretch uses a PVC pipe or broomstick held overhead to provide a fixed length while you bend to the side. The stick keeps the arms in line and forces the lats to stretch fully on the bent side. It is a great mobility tool used by Olympic lifters and overhead athletes.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a PVC stick overhead with hands wider than shoulder-width.
Lock the arms straight overhead.
Brace your core and keep your hips square.
Lean your torso to one side, reaching the stick to the side.
Feel a deep stretch in the lat on the opposite side.
Hold the position and breathe deeply.
Return to center and bend to the other side.
Deeply stretches the lats
Improves overhead mobility
Useful for Olympic lifters
Opens the side of the torso
Easy to do anywhere with a stick

description.en: The strongman power stairs is a competition event where athletes carry heavy implements (kegs, stones, or other objects) up a series of large steps. Each step is typically 12 to 24 inches tall. It tests leg strength, grip, and conditioning under heavy load.

en: Stand at the base of the power stairs with the implement at your feet.
Pick up the implement using a deadlift or bear hug grip.
Step up onto the first step with the implement.
Continue stepping up each successive step while holding the implement.
Place the implement on the top platform.
Return for the next implement and repeat.
Move as fast as possible — this is a timed event.
Specialized strongman equipment required.
Builds extreme leg strength under load
Tests grip and carrying endurance
Strongman competition event
Develops step-up power
Builds mental toughness
Full-body conditioning

description.en: The suspension trainer mountain climber is a TRX cardio core drill. The lifter places the feet in foot cradles and from a plank rapidly drives the knees toward the chest in alternating mountain climbers. The suspended feet add instability and a brutal core challenge.

en: Set the suspension trainer foot cradles low.
Place the feet in the foot cradles facing down.
Set the hands on the floor under the shoulders in a plank.
Brace your core hard and keep the body in a straight line.
Drive one knee toward the chest.
Extend that leg back and drive the other knee toward the chest.
Continue the alternating climber pattern at speed.
Keep the hips low and the core braced.
Brutal cardio core move
Strong TRX drill
Trains hip flexors
Builds shoulder stability
Strong conditioning move
Useful core finisher

description.en: The swimmer exercise lies face down and alternates lifting opposite arm and opposite leg in a fluttering pattern — like freestyle swimming on dry land. It builds posterior chain endurance, lower back strength, and coordination.

en: Lie face down with arms extended overhead and legs straight.
Simultaneously lift your right arm and left leg a few inches off the floor.
Lower them while simultaneously lifting your left arm and right leg.
Continue alternating in a smooth flutter pattern.
Keep your neck neutral — look at the floor.
Move with control and rhythm.
Continue for 20 to 30 seconds or 15 to 20 alternations.
Breathe steadily throughout.
Builds posterior chain endurance
Strengthens the lower back and glutes
Develops coordination between opposite limbs
No equipment needed
Beginner-friendly
Useful warm-up or rehab exercise

description.en: The weighted floor crunch feet on bench is a loaded core exercise that crunches the upper abs with feet on a bench. Holding a weight on the chest increases the demand on the abs while protecting the lower back.

en: Lie on your back on the floor with legs resting on a bench.
Knees should be bent at 90 degrees with calves parallel to the floor.
Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against the chest with both hands.
Brace the core and exhale as you crunch up.
Lift the shoulder blades off the floor while keeping the lower back down.
Squeeze the abs hard at the top of the crunch.
Lower the shoulders back to the floor with control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Hammers the upper abs with added load.
Bench position protects the lower back.
Easy to scale by changing the weight.
Builds visible ab strength and definition.
Strict tempo improves core control.
Carryover to compound lifts requiring strong abs.

description.en: The weighted floor twisting crunch feet on bench combines load, rotation, and an elevated leg position. The twist hits the obliques while the weight increases the demand on the upper abs.

en: Lie on your back on the floor with legs resting on a bench.
Knees bent at 90 degrees with calves parallel to the floor.
Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against the chest with both hands.
Brace the core and exhale as you crunch up.
As you lift, twist the torso so one shoulder points toward the opposite knee.
Squeeze the obliques hard at the top of the twist.
Lower back to the floor with control and untwist to neutral.
Alternate sides on each repetition.
Hits the obliques through controlled rotation under load.
Strengthens the upper abs in the crunch.
Bench position protects the lower back.
Easy to scale weight as needed.
Builds rotational core strength.
Improves twisting power for athletic carryover.

description.en: The weighted one hand pull up is an elite advanced back move. The lifter grips the bar with one hand and adds weight via a dip belt or weighted vest, then pulls the body up. The combination of unilateral work and added load is a brutal lat builder.

en: Add weight to a dip belt or wear a weighted vest.
Grip a pull up bar with one hand only.
Hang from the bar with the arm fully extended.
Brace your core and keep the body steady.
Pull the chin up over the bar by bending the elbow.
Squeeze the lat and bicep hard at the top.
Lower back down with control to a full hang.
Complete reps and switch hands.
Elite back builder
Strong unilateral pull
Builds extreme lat strength
Trains the biceps
Useful for advanced trainees
Builds back size
